newsitem.title: USA: Wall St. sees Washington support of merger boom.
newsitem.headline: Wall St. sees Washington support of merger boom.

text.p: The Justice Department's blessing of the giant Bell Atlantic-Nynex merger reinforces views on Wall Street that Washington generally approves of the merger boom sweeping Corporate America.

Still reeling from the government's recent rejection of a planned union between office supply chains Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc., merger experts said Thursday's action reflected the traditional process used to assess a mega-deal.
"I think they are legitimately looking at issues with the notion of becoming more competitive in industries where there's global competition," said one investment banker.
Originally valued at $23 billion, the Bell Atlantic Corp. merger with Nynex Corp. is now worth about $20 billion due to stock price fluctuations.
Most mergers are reviewed by the Justice Department or Federal Trade Commission, which study the transactions to see if they violate antitrust laws.

In approving the Bell Atlantic-Nynex deal, the Justice Department determined the merger would not block competition in the telecommunications business. The department did not impose any conditions on the merger.

"The Department of Justice looked at this in a traditional way and decided the merger did not represent an anticompetitive situation for consumers. I think the government did what most people expected," said one trader of takeover stocks.
But that's not always the case.
Although the bulk of today's corporate transaction clear regulatory hurdles quite easily, some recent deals have been foiled or dramatically changed by government disapproval.

Drugstore giant Rite Aid Corp. last year was forced to withdraw its $1.8 billion bid for rival Revco D.S. Inc. after authorities expressed concern about store overlap. Also last year, the Federal Trade Commission approved the union of pharmaceutical firms Ciba Geigy and Sandoz only after ordering a $780 million divestiture.

"My experience has been that every once in a while (regulators) will get stuck on something. And when they get stuck, they're stuck. It always adds unpredictability to a deal," said the investment banker.

The issue of antitrust often hinges on existing competition vs. future competition, experts said. In the case of Bell Atlantic and Nynex, regulators had to determine the future ability of telephone companies to vie against two firms that now do not compete with each other.
But the union of Staples and Office Depot would bring together two existing rivals and potentially make it tougher for other industry players to compete against them, they said.

"It's a lot easier to draw conclusions based on market information in a case where you have current competitors vs. where you have to think about potential competitors," said Dennis Yao, a former FTC commissioner who now specialises in antitrust at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.
Many industry experts believe that antitrust concerns helped prompt the end of a five-month takeover battle for control of Conrail Inc. by rivals CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp.

The two railroads, which have agreed to a $10.3 billion joint purchase of Conrail, had received preliminary indications that regulators might balk at the prospect of one carrier dominating East Coast rail freight.
"Whenever you see something like Staples-Office Depot, people worry for six months, but if 10 more large deals get done, you start forgetting about it," the banker said.
